idiom_name: nullable types (T?) with safe call ?., Elvis ?: and smart casts
implementation_notes: Kotlin puts nullability in the type system: a variable of type T is non-nullable, T? is nullable, and the compiler refuses member access on a nullable receiver except through a safe call (?. which yields null), a non-null assertion (!! which throws) or a smart cast after an explicit check; ?: supplies the default. The compiler's only documented sources of NullPointerException are the explicit throw, !!, initialisation leaks and Java interop, so the classic Maybe wrapper is unnecessary for the ordinary 'may be missing' case. Two boundaries stay leaky: Java interop introduces platform types whose nullability is unknown, and Java code can put null into a Kotlin collection that declares non-null element types. Arrow's Option is the wrapper alternative when absence must be a value with its own combinators.
code_sketch:
data class Address(val city: String)
data class Customer(val address: Address?)
data class Order(val customer: Customer?)

fun cityOf(order: Order): String =
    order.customer?.address?.city ?: "unknown"    // safe calls + Elvis default

fun cityOrNull(order: Order): String? =
    order.customer?.address?.city                 // or keep the absence in the type
pitfalls: !! is a runtime crash waiting for the input that violates an invariant; treat it as a documented assertion, never as a conversion.
Java interop creates platform types (String!) that can be used either way, so a missing annotation turns a NullPointerException back into a runtime surprise.
Nullable types cannot nest: T?? is not a type, so 'outer absence' and 'inner absence' are indistinguishable without a wrapper.
Smart casts need a stable val or a local copy; a nullable var mutated elsewhere refuses to smart-cast and pushes call sites back to !!.

variants.name: Arrow Option
variants.implementation_notes: Arrow models absence as a datatype rather than as a nullable type: Option<A> is Some<A> or None, with map/fold/getOrElse, exhaustive when matching, Option.fromNullable and toOption() for the boundary, and conversions to Either/computation blocks. Choose it where the code base already uses Arrow's typed-error stack, or where an Option must nest, be stored in data structures and be told apart from 'a nullable value'; plain nullable types remain the idiomatic default for parameters, fields and simple returns.
variants.code_sketch:
import arrow.core.Option
import arrow.core.Some
import arrow.core.none

val city: Option<String> = Some("Berlin")
val label = city.fold({ "unknown" }, { it.uppercase() })
val fromNullable: Option<String> = Option.fromNullable(javaValue)
pitfalls: Two vocabularies for the same absence (T? and Option<A>) in one code base: convert at module boundaries with toOption()/getOrNull() and pick one per layer.
Arrow is an external dependency whose API moves across major versions; pin the version and keep the conversions in one adapter.
